The table follows the path of the chapter. The first group splits a video into shots, the units that give a search result its edges. The classical detectors compare histograms of consecutive frames with one or two thresholds; a learned detector replaces the hand-tuned rules but keeps the threshold. The second group describes motion. With a static camera, differences between images reveal the moving objects, and the motion history image summarizes their movement into a feature; with a moving camera, optical flow estimates where each pixel moves, first with Lucas-Kanade at corners and today with learned models for every pixel. The third group knows concepts: image embeddings for what is visible, video models for what happens, and video-language models that answer questions. A practical system combines all three groups on the common time line of the video, with cheap methods scanning everything and expensive models inspecting only the candidates.

The shot is the basic retrieval unit of video. Histogram distances between consecutive frames detect hard cuts, because histograms ignore where a color occurs and therefore tolerate motion within a shot. The threshold comes from the distance distributions within and across shots, and for retrieval a missed cut costs more than a false one.

Gradual transitions spread the change over many frames. Twin thresholds detect them by comparing the frames before and after the change, which differ as much as the two sides of a hard cut, even when every single step is small.

With a static camera, background subtraction and frame differencing find moving objects, each with its own failures. The motion history image accumulates the masks into a fading trail that turns motion into a feature vector for retrieval.

Optical flow follows from brightness constancy, which gives one equation per pixel for two unknowns: the aperture problem. Lucas-Kanade solves it by assuming a common motion in a small window, which works where the window contains gradients in different directions, that is, at corners.

Current video search embeds sampled frames with CLIP, pools them per shot, and fuses the visual ranking with transcripts, OCR, and audio events that share the time line. Cheap detectors propose candidate moments, expensive models confirm them, and shot boundaries set the edges of the clip.

Learned models improve on the classical methods, but they do not remove their hard cases. On “Tears of Steel”, TransNet V2 reaches an F1 score of 0.96 against 0.75 for twin thresholds, yet both miss the same two dissolves. RAFT estimates the flow of every pixel, at hundreds of times the cost of Lucas-Kanade. CLIP finds robots but not a fight, and the wording of the query matters more than the pooling.
